items.title: ‘I Know God’s Power’: Dallas Jenkins Reacts Moments After Filming Last-Ever ‘The Chosen’ Scene
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The end of an era.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

“The Chosen” creator Dallas Jenkins was filled with gratitude last Thursday night just moments after filming the final scene of his popular biblical series.

Jenkins, who exclusively invited CBN News on set in Texas to witness those last moments, expressed his profound gratitude for how the show is coming to an end.

“I feel awesome because there’s no more days hanging over my head, no more seasons hanging over my head, we’ve done the work that we set out to go,” he said. “God provided everything that we needed.”

The last scene, which featured the disciples on a boat, was memorable because the vessel used in filming was the same seen in the first season of the show. The scene offered a literal and figurative full-circle moment.

“God has met us here in the waters so often,” Jenkins said. “I have nothing but gratitude.”

Ultimately, Jenkins said the mission behind the show has never changed, even as the audience has swelled to over 100 million people.

“We haven’t changed,” he said. “We’re still trying to do the work for God. We’re still humbled, we’re still surrendered, we’re still grinding.”

As for how the seven-season journey changed Jenkins, he said it offered him insight into God’s character and relationship with mankind.

“I’ve been a believer as long as I can remember,” he said. “I know God’s power. … I don’t think I knew quite as much as I do now from doing this show how intimate of a God He is, how personal of a God he is.”

items.title: How Hunting for Deer Helped One Man Overcome His Wife’s Cancer Diagnosis
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Though many years apart, James Hampton learned similar lessons about God, first through a cancer battle and later when he harvested a 150-inch buck on a hunting trip.

James and his twin brother Chad, now both pastors, grew up in a Christian home and were early followers of Jesus — and quick studies in the deer stand, too. As kids, hunting was a hobby that quickly blossomed into something more, and ultimately became the vehicle for their evangelistic mission today.

“During my wife’s cancer battle, God really spoke to both of us through that battle,” James said during a recent appearance on CBN’s “Faith in Culture” podcast, noting he and his wife were particularly drawn to James 1:2-3, where it’s written, “Dear brothers and sisters, when troubles of any kind come your way, consider it an opportunity for great joy. For you know that when your faith is tested, your endurance has a chance to grow” (NLT).

He continued, “That’s what God does through the waiting, through the trials, through the hard times, and definitely through the cancer battle that my wife went through. He really created perseverance in us, and it’s the same way in hunting.”

At first, that may seem like a peculiar connection — particularly to people who have never hunted.

But, as James said, “there’s a lot of waiting involved in hunting.” The same is true, at times, of waiting for God’s answers to prayer.

The preacher explained he put in more than 100 hours of waiting in the tree stand and, once the timing lined up just right, it was only a matter of seconds — 10, to be exact — before it was all over: he and Chad finally nabbed a 150-inch buck.

“It’s the same way on our hunt for God,” said James. “There’s so much waiting and patience and perseverance.”

As guys with a knack for hunting, they feel naturally at home using sportsman’s language to understand their faith. In fact, their organization, Huntin’ the Truth Ministries, was born out of that correlation.

King David’s writing in Psalm 14:2 has become an anchor for their ministry. In it, he wrote, “The Lord looks down from heaven on the entire human race; he looks to see if anyone is truly wise, if anyone seeks God” (NLT).

The Hampton twins, co-authors of the new devotional, “100 Days of Strength for Hunters,” interpret David’s writing through their passion for hunting. Strong’s Concordance defines “seek” as “investigate,” “enquire,” “study,” “practice,” and “follow.”

“God looks down from heaven on all of us, the sons of men, to see if there are any who understand or any who hunt for Him,” James said.

It was James’ wife’s fight against cancer that God used to bring that Psalm to James’ mind. He said, “[I was] hunting for my own plan for so long.” It wasn’t until he reached the end of himself, he said, that James found himself in the tree stand one night, where he started talking to God about his fears and frustration.

When he’s out hunting, James said, he always carries a small camo Bible in his backpack. He opened the Scriptures and God guided him to Psalm 14.

“It was that night God kind of slapped me across the face and made me realize … that He wanted me to hunt for Him like I hunt for deer,” James recalled. “He wants us all to hunt for Him, to search for Him, to seek for Him. … And I knew what He was talking about, because I knew how much of a diehard hunter I was and how much passion I had for hunting and how many hours I put in for hunting.”

He added, “God was telling me, ‘I want you to do the same thing: I want you to hunt for Me that hard. Seek Me that hard, with all your heart.'”

items.title: If Jesus Didn’t Do It Alone, Maybe We Shouldn’t Either, Says Toni Collier
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: When a mentor told Toni Collier to start praying for friends, she thought it sounded like something a kid would pray. “What a weak, weird prayer,” she remembers thinking. “What am I, a child?” When Collier started following Jesus in earnest, she wanted to quit cursing, drinking and doing drugs. She
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

When a mentor told Toni Collier to start praying for friends, she thought it sounded like something a kid would pray. “What a weak, weird prayer,” she remembers thinking. “What am I, a child?”

When Collier started following Jesus in earnest, she wanted to quit cursing, drinking and doing drugs. She said spending time with her old friends kept drawing her back into habits she wanted to leave. “I ended up alone,” she told RELEVANT.

Asking for friends went against the way Collier had learned to move through life. She said she left her parents’ house at 16, finished college at 19 and later earned a master’s degree. She was used to moving quickly and taking care of herself. “I’m fast. I’m capable. I got it. That’s what I thought of myself. I can handle it.”

After she started praying, Collier found herself working up the nerve to introduce herself to a stranger. At a church conference, she noticed a woman in the green room with platinum blonde hair and tattoos up her arm. Collier thought they looked like complete opposites, but she felt drawn to talk to her.

“I just felt like I needed to go talk to her,” she said. “It was awkward. So awkward.”

They’ve been friends for nine years. When Collier went through a public divorce she described as humiliating, that woman was the first person she called. Her friend had been through a divorce too, and understood what it was like to keep going in ministry afterward. The relationship Collier once felt silly asking God for had become one she depended on.

The Strong Friend

Collier knows how much pride can get tangled up in being the person who can handle everything. In the interview, she described the shame that kept her from admitting she needed people, even as she wanted them close. Asking could mean finding out that someone didn’t want to stay.

“I don’t want to be needy because then I’ll be discounted,” she said. “I don’t want to need people because maybe they won’t come back because they’ll get tired of me.”

She had carried that fear into her understanding of strength. Then her own life became more than she could manage by herself. “And now we look stupid because we don’t have anybody around us to catch us when we are no longer the strong friend,” she said.

It’s an expectation she has trouble reconciling with Jesus’ life. The Gospels describe him gathering disciples and living alongside friends. For Collier, that example gives Christians room to need each other without treating dependence as a failure of faith.

“Jesus did not need the 12 disciples to fulfill the purpose that was on the inside of him,” she said. “And yet he still did it with people, probably to teach us all that if Jesus didn’t do it alone, maybe we shouldn’t either.”

In her own friendships, accepting help has sometimes meant letting someone introduce her to something she hadn’t known to ask for. Collier said counseling wasn’t familiar to her growing up. A friend named Erin asked who her counselor was, treating the question as casually as asking about a trainer at the gym. Their conversation helped her see professional support as something she could seek.

She also turns to friends with more years behind them. Now in her mid-30s, she described calling friends in their 50s and 60s when she faced something unfamiliar. They had lived through situations she was encountering for the first time. Those relationships gave her people she could ask, “What would you do in this situation?”

Someone Who Can Stay

Letting friends into a painful part of your life comes with a question of its own: what will they do once they know? Collier is wary of the impulse to immediately offer an answer. She recognizes it in herself, especially when she wants to help someone through a hard season.

“I love a good redemption story and I want to be a part,” she said. “We’re not God and we are no one’s savior.”

At the time of the interview, she had been reading Job. What held her attention was the beginning of his friends’ visit: they heard about his suffering, traveled to him and sat on the ground with him for seven days and nights without speaking. She had expected them to arrive with resources to rebuild his life. Their first response was to sit with him.

“When someone’s in pain, when someone’s suffering, they really just need witness,” she said. “They need their friends to be there.”

She uses that word in her book, Don’t Try This Alone, borrowing from her group therapy circle’s description of witness as “the art of being with someone in their pain.” In John 11, she sees it in Jesus weeping with those mourning Lazarus before raising him from the dead. “I think Jesus was trying to show us something much more important than him answering all of our prayers, that he’s with us,” she said.

For a friend listening to someone describe a lost job or difficulty having a baby, that can mean resisting the rush to recommend a devotional or offer a doctor’s number. Collier suggests starting with “I’m really sorry,” and acknowledging how much it hurts. There will be problems a friend can’t solve. The friendship still gives them a way to be present.

Collier doesn’t make opening up sound painless. “Vulnerability really sucks sometimes,” she said. She compared it to uncovering wounds she had spent years trying to hide. Being willing to do that requires friends she trusts to keep her confidence and stay involved after the conversation gets difficult.

“We’re not looking for safe spaces. We’re looking for safe people,” she said. “People that won’t go tell your business. People that can show up for you.”

Finding them takes some ordinary, uncomfortable effort. Collier recommends places where people gather regularly, including church, and making yourself available for a conversation. Her own prayer for friends led her into a room where she still had to walk over and say hello.

“I had to start conversations or be open to conversations that were being had with me,” she said. “That’s on me. That’s on us. We got to start getting brave enough to say, ‘What’s your name? You live around here? You have kids?’”

Years later, when her marriage ended, she had someone she could call who already knew her. She didn’t have to explain what continuing in ministry after a divorce might feel like. Her friend had been there.

items.title: The Feast of the Little Flower, St. Thérèse of Lisieux
items.author: Fr. Steve Grunow
items.summary:
Fr. Steve Grunow

Today marks a great day for the Church and Word on Fire in particular: the feast day of St. Thérèse of Lisieux, one of the great patrons of the ministry.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Fr. Steve Grunow

On September 30, 1897, a young Carmelite nun living in France succumbed to the effects of tuberculosis, dying in obscurity, known only to her sisters in religious life.

Like many Carmelite nuns before her, Thérèse’s death should have meant the culmination of a life of obscurity, freely chosen, so that one might disappear fully into the mission of the Church. Yet this particular Carmelite would prove different in this respect. Within years of her death, the spiritual autobiography of St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus of the Holy Face would captivate the Church. Miracles attributed to her intercession began to be reported. In just a few decades after her death, the image of Thérèse of Lisieux would be immediately recognizable in the Catholic world. Canonization would soon follow. At the hundred year anniversary of her death, Pope John Paul II declared this formerly obscure Carmelite nun to be one of the Doctors of the Church, a title given to only a privileged few of the Church’s saints. This title established St. Thérèse as one of the Church’s great authorities in regards to the meaning and purpose of the Christian spiritual life.

At the heart of Thérèse’s understanding of the spiritual life is the principle that holiness can be appreciated and accomplished not only in the performance of mighty deeds but in a willing surrender to the purposes of God as we engage the seemingly ordinary experiences of life. This means that the possibility of communion with the holiness of Christ will be found for most not in accomplishments worthy of the world’s or even the Church’s attention, but in a hidden, unnoticed practice of receptivity to how Christ presents himself to us in the day to day circumstances of our lives.

This might sound so obvious that one might dismiss it as being trite. However, think carefully about the implications.

The great test of the spiritual way is coming to terms with the startling truth that we don’t get to choose on what occasion that Christ might meet us. We don’t get to decide for ourselves just where and when Christ will make his presence known.

Our mission is to prepare ourselves to receive Christ on his terms and in accord with his purposes. It is in our willingness to do this that his holiness is accomplished in us. Because this is one of the great truths of the spiritual life, we discover that one does not have to journey into the desert as a hermit to know the challenges of asceticism. One does not have to journey to lands hostile to the Faith and suffer martyrdom to know what it means to suffer for the sake of the Gospel. Opportunities to know and serve the Lord will find us, wherever we are, and when they do, will we rise to the occasion seek to serve the Lord?

St. Thérèse’s personal appropriation of her spiritual way culminated in the manner in which she experienced suffering and death. Beset by physical discomfort, she was overtaken by an intense, spiritual darkness. She accepted these as being opportunities to know the Lord and to grow in faith, hope, and love.

What spiritual lesson does the witness of St. Thérèse offer us?

Perhaps we might consider whether too much of our prayer is dedicated to pleading for exemptions from the hard facts and difficult circumstances of life. We tell the Lord what we do not want to face, what we just couldn’t accept, rather than coming to terms with the truth that God delivers and redeems us not from the reality of human existence but through it. God will not take us anywhere that he didn’t go himself, this much we know from the revelation of Christ. St. Thérèse shows us that it is within an embrace of the reality of our existence that the Lord reveals himself and teaches us his truth.

May St. Thérèse intercede for us and help us to be attentive to the presence of Christ in all the experiences of life.

This piece first appeared on Evangelization & Culture Online on October 1, 2013.

items.title: Potentiality and Sexual Ethics
items.author: Henry Long
items.summary:
Henry Long

Learning about the concept of metaphysical potentiality will equip socially conservative collegians to more effectively defend traditional moral positions on abortion, gender, and sexuality.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Henry Long

Learning about the concept of metaphysical potentiality will equip socially conservative collegians to more effectively defend traditional moral positions on abortion, gender, and sexuality.

As college freshmen across the country begin their first weeks of classes, contentious debates around sexual ethics will arise in dorms, dining halls, and classrooms. Many social conservatives will arrive at predominantly liberal campuses ill-equipped to defend their moral convictions. If these conservative undergraduates do not succumb to the all-too-common trend of self-censorship, they will be asked to give an account for their apparently retrogressive beliefs about abortion, gender, and sexuality. While some may be able to marshal a slogan or muster a simple argument, most will be unprepared to weather sustained cross-examination about the rational foundation of their controversial beliefs.

For these young traditionalists, much of their moral formation may have been reinforced by their religious or social milieu. Faced with a difficult argument, these students may appeal to sentiment, intuition, or religious dogma. This tactic is unlikely to persuade an interlocutor, especially on secular campuses. Moreover, this maneuver buttresses the interlocutor’s suspicion that those who hold these beliefs are bigoted rubes who harbor prejudice toward women, gay people, and transgender individuals.

If the social positions held by these students truly are irrational and hateful, then they should abandon them. But just because these beliefs are difficult to defend or have disquieting implications does not necessarily mean they are wrong. As someone who once stood in these students’ shoes, I wish someone would have taken me aside to carefully explicate the metaphysical and moral principles that undergird socially conservative positions on sexual ethics. Below, I hope to offer such an explication to incoming undergraduates.

In my experience, basic familiarity with simple metaphysical concepts goes a long way toward blunting some of the most common objections to traditional positions on sexual ethics. Specifically, many of the difficulties in defending traditional beliefs around sex and gender stem from an unfamiliarity with the oft-overlooked but important, technical but intuitive concept of potentiality. By learning this one piece of conceptual machinery, the contemporary conservative collegian can acquire a more effective way to defend traditional social positions and a richer understanding of human nature to boot.

Potentiality is a concept first explained by the Greek philosopher Aristotle and later developed by thinkers like St. Thomas Aquinas. For these philosophers, potentiality, also called potency, is defined as the real capacity for some act. While the definition sounds technical, examples are intuitive. An acorn has the potentiality to become a tree, and a fish has the potentiality to swim. But an acorn does not have the potentiality to swim, and a fish does not have the potentiality to become a tree. Having a potentiality means more than being theoretically possible or conceivable. A potentiality is a power inherent in a particular type of thing, and this power is always directed toward a particular state of being or acting. 

The potentialities of a thing are deeply intertwined with the kind of thing that it is. In other words, we can determine what something is by discovering the potentialities it has, and vice versa. For example, in chemistry, it may be hard to see the chemical structure of a particular molecule, but scientists can determine what a molecule is by determining the potentialities it has to react to various stimuli. In biology, scientists can determine what species an organism is by examining the potentialities it has for various functions.

The concept of potentiality clarifies many ideas that are obscured in contemporary discourse. Disability is a great example. While many of us are generally familiar with the idea of disability and know persons with disabilities, the concept can be hard to define. A disability is clearly the absence of some ability—but what kind of ability? Human beings cannot fly, but this inability is not a disability. Perhaps an inability that is not shared by the majority of humans? But if a global environmental pollutant gave everyone anosmia (the inability to smell), anosmia would still be a disability even though the majority of humans had it.

The concept of potentiality helps answer the question. A disability is the absence of some ability for which human beings have a potentiality, like sight or hearing. This potentiality is inherent in the kind of thing that humans are, and the failure to realize any of these potentialities constitutes a disability.

On the issue of gender, conservatives will rightly volley the “What is a woman?” gotcha question to stump supporters of transgenderism. But conservatives are often ill prepared to answer when the question is turned around on them. When answering, conservatives often err by appealing to some fully actual trait, characteristic, or body part that all women are supposed to have, like vaginas, uteruses, XX chromosomes, or ova. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

But the problem is that not all women actually have these traits. This leaves the conservative vulnerable to several retorts: Are people who have had hysterectomies not women? Are people with Swyer syndrome not women? Are people with primary ovarian insufficiency not women? Instead, to truly get a clear understanding of what a woman is, we must turn to her potentialities. As Notre-Dame professor Abigail Favale writes in her cogent book, The Genesis of Gender,

A woman is the kind of human being whose body is organized around the potential to gestate new life. This potentiality that belongs to femaleness is always present, even if there is some kind of condition, such as age or disease, that prevents that potential from being actualized.

A question here arises: If a woman is infertile, does she not lose the potentiality to gestate new life? Here, it is worth distinguishing between two kinds of potentialities. I do not currently know how to play the guitar, but as a human being, I have the potential to learn how to do so. This kind of fundamental potentiality, based on the kind of thing something is, is called first potentiality. Notably, the first potentiality for an action remains even when the specific body parts that make the action possible are temporarily or even permanently damaged. My first potentiality to play the guitar remains even if my fingers are temporarily broken or permanently amputated. This kind of potentiality is distinguished from second potentiality, which can be called into action at a moment’s notice. If I were to learn how to play the guitar, I would have the potential to play the guitar at any time and thereby have a second potentiality to play the guitar.

Thus, an infertile woman may have permanently lost her second potentiality to conceive and gestate new life, just as a non-ovulating woman has temporarily lost her second potentiality to conceive and gestate new life. Regardless, in both of these situations, the woman nonetheless retains a first potentiality to do so based on the kind of creature that she is. The point becomes even clearer when we consider the sex binary. No matter the hormonal or surgical interventions, a woman will never have the potentiality to impregnate, just as a man will never have the potentiality to conceive and gestate new life.

Speaking of conceiving and gestating new life, potentiality is also relevant to debates around abortion. Specifically, potentiality has a bearing on the question of whether a fetus is a full human being deserving of moral respect. As with gender, debates around the personhood of fetuses often center around the question of actual traits the fetus possesses. Does it have a heartbeat? The ability to feel pain? Viability? Brain activity? Consciousness? At any given moment of prenatal development, it may be possible to say no to any of these questions. Some abortion advocates will take this fact as proof that at these stages of life, the fetus is not human, and it is therefore permissible to end its life.

But this thinking is mistaken when you understand human beings from the perspective of potentiality. As a rational animal, human beings—fetuses included—necessarily have a first potentiality for rational thought. That said, at a particular moment, a particular human—whether a healthy fetus or an adult with a disability—might lack the second potentiality for rational thought. But for disabled people as well as fetuses, this lack of second potentiality makes them no less human. Under normal conditions, human fetuses are the kind of things that have the potential to develop into fully able human adults. Thus, when considered in light of potentiality, it becomes clear that fetuses, like persons with disabilities, are no less human than you and I.

As should be clear from the issues above, potentiality is relevant to our moral obligations. Potentiality helps elucidate what something is, and what something is has implications for what we should (and should not) do to it. In the case of gender, the potential for gestation shows that a human being is a female, and one should not suppress the natural development of female puberty except under grave medical circumstances. In the case of fetuses, the potential for rational thought shows that a fetus is a human being, and one should not intentionally kill an innocent human being.

In both of these cases, the moral principle at play involves a respect for the potentialities of the human body. If a human potentiality exists for some specific end, then humans should never intentionally actualize that potentiality in a way that perverts that end. Put otherwise, human beings should not intentionally actualize human potentialities only to frustrate them. This principle has bearings on other principles of traditional sexual ethics like the proscriptions of contraception, IVF, masturbation, sodomy, incest, necrophilia, bestiality, fornication, and adultery—all of which intentionally pervert the proper potentiality of the sexual act.

Some clarifications are in order. First, to be immoral, the perversion of these potentialities must be intentional. Sophocles’s tragedy Oedipus Rex provides examples of this principle. Tiresias, the congenitally blind seer, is not culpable for his blindness, but Oedipus, who gouges his eyes out, is. Oedipus procreating with his mother Jocasta is wrong because it violates the proper potentiality of the sexual faculty, but Oedipus is not morally culpable because he did not know Jocasta was his mother.

Second, the requirement that one should not frustrate human potentialities comes with a caveat called the principle of totality and integrity. This principle states that humans may frustrate lower-order potentialities when it is medically necessary to preserve the integrity of the whole human being. For example, during the Civil War, doctors often had to amputate legs with bullet wounds to ensure that infection would not spread to the rest of the body. This was a permissible frustration of the leg’s potential because this potential could not be saved without losing the potential of the whole body.

No doubt these arguments and ideas are controversial, but they are arguments and not simply appeals to emotion or authority. A short article will be unable to resolve all possible objections to these arguments. That said, introducing the simple but versatile concept of potentiality will hopefully enable conservative undergraduates to dig deeper and elevate the discourse beyond simple sloganeering. Ideally, a ressourcement of potentiality and the rich metaphysical tradition that birthed it will inspire renewed and sustained reflection on the intricacies of our bodies and the purpose for which they are made.
